top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on the common test. Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices changed what can be credibly measured about substitution, markups, market power and merger effects. About three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, regulation and other fields have exposed its limits. The citation can be confined to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which the three names share as one jointly authored contribution. No prior-prize overlap has been raised against it. The main reservations are that it is a methods prize without a single headline finding, that estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, and that the three-name cap excludes Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I treat these as limits on the wording, which should not claim settled magnitudes or the dynamic-industry strand, and not as bars. Colleague support counts are not evidence of merit. I have not independently verified the claims about use, replication or prior prizes. P002 (B030: Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is a strong design-based substantive contribution, but its persistence, magnitude and shift-share debates make it less settled. It ranks above no award because it is a credible, well-attributed candidate. No award ranks last because P001 clearly meets the bar.
recusal_note: Field proximity: my research is in industrial organisation and pricing, which is close to B005 and may bias me toward it. I applied a stated common test to counter this. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn, or to Autor, Dorn or Hanson. I have co-authored with committee colleagues John Hassler (chair) and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). These ties concern committee relationships, not a candidate. My spouse's public political role has no apparent bearing. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
